title: The AI Trade Deconstructed: AI Builders, AI Suppliers and AI Product firms!
gist: After the Nov 5 selloff (NASDAQ about -6%, about $1.8T AI market cap lost), Damodaran argues 'the AI trade' should be split into suppliers, builders, product firms and customers whose interests are diverging, with chips and electrical suppliers hit first and hyperscalers resilient. He sees a 'big market delusion' and shows the Anthropic IPO valuation falling to about $1.25T under higher compute and regulatory costs.

insights.claim: Damodaran splits the AI ecosystem into suppliers (chips, electrical equipment, power, real estate), builders/hyperscalers (Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, plus Oracle and Coreweave), product firms (OpenAI, Anthropic, Palantir, SpaceX) and customers, whose interests increasingly diverge.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Treating 'the AI trade' as one basket is no longer adequate; each group needs its own valuation lens.

insights.claim: The same AI capex is a revenue and profit for suppliers, a cash-flow and earnings drag (via amortization) for builders, and an operating or financial (imputed interest plus depreciation) expense for product firms leasing the capacity.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: One dollar of capex lands very differently across income statements, so group-level earnings and multiples are not comparable.

insights.claim: The assumed life of AI infrastructure determines the amortization schedule and hence current-year earnings of builders, making depreciation lives a key accounting debate.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Longer assumed lives flatter builder earnings; watch for changes in depreciation policy.

insights.claim: Circular financing is pervasive: Microsoft and Nvidia are shareholders in OpenAI, Alphabet and Amazon in Anthropic, and Nvidia has provided financial backstops for data centers, creating accounting noise from equity mark-ups and opacity.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Reported earnings at AI firms may include mark-ups on stakes in each other; quality of earnings is lower than it looks.
insights.quote: Microsoft and Nvidia are shareholders in OpenAI, Alphabet and Amazon in Anthropic and Nvidia has also provided financial backstops for data centers being built out

insights.claim: Stronger players like Nvidia finance or guarantee weaker ecosystem members to ensure survival and sustain investment spending, because pain in one group spreads to the others.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Circular financing is a contagion channel: a failure at the weak end can hit the strong supplier.

insights.claim: Collective AI product and service revenue is only about $250 billion even using leaked ARR figures, small relative to what has been invested.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: The ecosystem rests on future customer adoption, not current revenue.
insights.quote: the collective revenues from AI products and services right now is about $250 billion

insights.claim: Benefits arrive in sequence: suppliers see revenue and profit first, builders next, and AI product companies are last to profitability.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Supplier outperformance is an early-cycle feature and does not validate end-market profitability.

insights.claim: In the business-building phase, supplier growth eases as new spend shrinks relative to base, builders push to bring supply in-house or find competitors compressing margins, and suppliers will look cheap on PE and EV multiples because the market prices lower growth.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Low multiples at suppliers may be a rational reflection of peak growth, not a bargain.

insights.claim: AI product companies face a duration problem: compute commitments are locked up long term while revenue streams are young and volatile, so their pricing looks high on current numbers and will be volatile.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Long fixed commitments against uncertain revenue raise default and renegotiation risk.

insights.claim: Three scenarios: AI works better than expected (product firms benefit first, then builders, then suppliers), as expected (some product firms gain at others' expense, weaker players drop out), or worse than expected (product firms break or renegotiate compute commitments, builders abandon capacity, suppliers suffer).
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Downside propagates upstream through compute contracts; suppliers are the most exposed to the bad scenario.

insights.claim: Competing interests will increasingly overwhelm common ones: builder overbuilding hurts builders but is a bonanza for suppliers, and builders favoring long leases raises default risk for product companies.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Expect divergent stock performance among groups, not uniform moves.

insights.claim: If history is a guide, product companies will be the primary beneficiaries of a large AI market, though the central role of compute may give builders and suppliers more of a share.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Value capture within the stack is unresolved.

insights.claim: Aggregate market cap of every AI group surged from 2022 to 2025, led by chips (Nvidia the largest contributor); builders lagged but still rose 180% despite hundreds of billions in capex with little visible return.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: The re-rating was broad-based, which is why undifferentiated AI exposure paid until now.
insights.locator: AI Companies - Letting the Data Speak!

insights.claim: AI companies' share of US equity market cap rose for most of 2026, peaking at about 37% on September 30, 2026, and every AI group except real estate and construction has struggled since the end of Q3.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Concentration at 37% of the market means AI drawdowns now move the whole index.
insights.locator: AI Companies - Letting the Data Speak!

insights.claim: In 2026 year to date, only AI chips and AI real estate ran ahead of the market while the other groups lagged, so strength in some groups masked weakness in others.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: The market was already discriminating before the November break.

insights.claim: On Thursday November 5 AI stocks lost almost $1.8 trillion in market cap, with chip stocks taking the brunt, while NASDAQ fell close to 6% and the S&P 500 about 4%.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Marks the sharpest test of the AI trade yet.

insights.claim: During the selloff week the AI chip and electrical groups were hit hardest while hyperscalers, including four Mag Seven names, saw aggregate market cap increase, showing the market already differentiates suppliers from builders.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Slower data center construction hurts suppliers first, while capex-weary builder shareholders may welcome it.
insights.quote: the hyperscalers, with the four Mag Seven companies in their midst, actually saw an aggregate increase in market cap during the week
insights.locator: AI Companies - Letting the Data Speak!

insights.claim: If post-election data center slowdowns materialize, shareholders in hyperscalers worried about capex magnitude may welcome the slowdown, since it reduces their cash burn.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Bad news for suppliers can be good news for builders' free cash flow.
insights.locator: AI Companies - Letting the Data Speak!

insights.claim: The AI sample has caveats: private leaders (OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, Qwen, Deepseek) are excluded, SpaceX joined mid-2026, firms are not pure plays, and some span groups, so the AI effect on hyperscaler market cap is hard to isolate.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Treat the product-group results with caution; only three companies are in it.
insights.locator: AI Companies - Letting the Data Speak!

insights.claim: SpaceX's AI arm earns almost all its revenue leasing compute to Anthropic and Alphabet, making it more an AI builder than an AI product company.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Classification shapes how SpaceX should be valued.
insights.locator: AI Companies - Letting the Data Speak!

themes.theme: Big market delusion and investor response

insights.claim: Damodaran argues AI almost certainly has led to over-investment by builders, over-commitment to compute by LLM firms and over-pricing by the market in aggregate, a pattern he calls the big market delusion, with a correction that will hurt unevenly.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: A correction is likely but its form and timing are unknowable.
insights.quote: I believe that AI, because of its reach and potential, almost certainly has led to over investment
insights.locator: An Assessment of AI as investment

insights.claim: Overbuilding and corrections are a feature of big change, not a bug, and are a prerequisite for it despite cleanup costs.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Correction pain does not imply the technology fails.
insights.locator: An Assessment of AI as investment

insights.claim: Because correction timing and catalysts are unpredictable and rooted in investor psychology, avoiding or shorting AI becomes market timing with questionable payoffs, and technical indicators may better detect mood shifts.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Do not dismiss price and volume signals entirely when sentiment drives the turn.
insights.locator: An Assessment of AI as investment

insights.claim: Long-term holders of AI winners should sell a portion on each correction phase, and post-correction buyers should set automatic limit buys at pre-chosen valuations rather than wait for a bottom, e.g. SpaceX at a $1 trillion market cap.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Rules-based trimming and pre-set entry prices replace timing.
insights.locator: Acting in the fact of uncertainty

insights.claim: The payoff to fundamental valuation is greatest where and when uncertainty is maximal, so AI bulls should use dark-mood periods like November 5 to become more discriminating.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Indiscriminate crisis selling creates opportunities in names that should not be marked down.

insights.claim: Both 'bubble' and 'sure win' priors are mistakes: a bubble view would have kept an investor out of a segment that added almost $18 trillion in market cap between 2023 and 2026, while sure-win thinking ignores that no equity win is certain.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Hold beliefs about AI loosely and differentiate by group.
insights.quote: would have kept you out of a segment that has added almost $18 trillion in market capitalization between 2023 and 2026

insights.claim: Damodaran sold all his Nvidia shares in four installments, the last earlier this year, after holding a twenty-bagger bought in 2018, and says he has no regrets.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Author disclosed trimming the chip leader into strength.

insights.claim: Rumors suggest the Anthropic IPO could be cut from an initial $1.5 to $2 trillion estimate or delayed into next year, as bankers fear overpricing a trillion-dollar-plus offering amid darker market mood.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: IPO pricing is a mood and momentum game and mood has soured.

insights.claim: A leak put Anthropic's October ARR at $80 billion, read as good news by some and bad news by others.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: ARR growth is the key pricing metric for the IPO.

insights.claim: Election results sent a clear voter message against data centers, and Texas hosts about a third of new data centers coming online, so growth in US data centers should slow and a new Congress may tighten AI regulation, dragging margins.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Policy risk is now a fundamental input to AI valuations, hitting suppliers first.

insights.claim: Data center limits could vindicate Anthropic's rush to lock in compute commitments and act as a moat against competitors.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Scarce compute may favor firms that contracted early.

insights.claim: Lowering Anthropic's sales-to-capital ratio from 3 to 2.5 and raising the regulatory margin drag from 5% to 7.5% cuts estimated equity value to $1.25 trillion, even with target revenues of a trillion dollars.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: The valuation is highly sensitive to compute intensity and regulation assumptions.
insights.quote: reduces the estimated equity value to $1.25 trillion

insights.claim: Damodaran expects the Anthropic IPO to proceed since withdrawal would signal worst cases, but would not be surprised by pricing closer to $1.25 trillion with a smaller cash raise to allow a first-day price jump.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Expect a downsized, cheaper IPO engineered for a pop.
